short_description: The largest subject in the atlas: an adult female Dirofilaria immitis nematode reaches 25-30 cm, lives coiled in the right ventricle and pulmonary arteries of dogs (and less often cats), and is transmitted only via mosquitoes carrying its ~300 µm first-stage larvae (microfilariae). NOT segmented like an earthworm; NOT a tapeworm/fluke (no suckers, hooks or scolex).

morphology_notes: Phylum Nematoda (roundworms): the body is a smooth, unsegmented cylinder covered by a collagenous cuticle with fine longitudinal striations — there are NO external rings/segments as in an earthworm (annelid) or a tapeworm's proglottids. This is the single most likely rendering error and must be actively guarded against.

Dirofilaria immitis is additionally distinguished by prominent muscular lateral cords that make the cuticle bulge slightly inward over them, giving a subtle longitudinal 'bat-wing' cross-section — a fine diagnostic detail, not a segmentation pattern, and not something to emphasize over the smooth overall silhouette.

Anterior end: blunt/tapered, with a small simple mouth opening directly into a muscular (filariform) esophagus — no jaws, teeth, hooks, suckers or scolex of any kind (those belong to tapeworms/flukes/hookworms, not filarial nematodes).

Marked sexual size dimorphism: adult females are the larger sex, 25-30 cm long (CDC DPDx gives 230-310 mm) by roughly 1 mm diameter; adult males are smaller, 15-18 cm (CDC DPDx gives 120-190 mm) by roughly 0.7-0.8 mm diameter.

Posterior end is the clearest sex marker: the female's tail is straight/simple, while the male's tail is characteristically coiled into a tight spiral (used to grip the female during mating, with copulatory spicules extended from the coiled end) — this is a mandatory, checkable feature whenever a male or a mating pair is shown.
A gravid (pregnant) female's body cavity is dominated internally by a paired, coiled reproductive tract (ovaries/uteri) that can occupy most of her internal volume — relevant for a textbook cutaway.
Colour: adults are white to cream/off-white and translucent, matching nematode cuticle generally (this is real colour, not a false-colour convention).

Adults live coiled together in a loose tangle in the right ventricle and the pulmonary arteries (main and lobar branches) — NOT the left heart. A worm burden can extend from the pulmonary arteries back into the right ventricle and even the right atrium/vena cava in heavy infections (caval syndrome).

Microfilariae (first-stage larvae, L1) are ~300 µm long (sources range 290-330 µm) by 6-7 µm wide, UNSHEATHED (no surrounding sheath membrane, unlike some other filarial species), with a tapered/pointed anterior end and a long, thin, sometimes hook-shaped tail. They circulate free in peripheral blood, are motile, and are what a mosquito ingests during a blood meal.

Life cycle: a mosquito bites an infected dog/cat and ingests circulating microfilariae -> these develop (two molts) into infective third-stage larvae (L3) inside the mosquito over about two weeks -> at the mosquito's next bite, L3 larvae enter the new host through the bite wound -> migrate through subcutaneous/muscle tissue, molting to L4 then to young adults (L5) over ~2-3 months -> immature adults enter the bloodstream and migrate to the pulmonary arteries and right heart, reaching sexual maturity roughly 6-7 months after the infective bite -> mated females release new microfilariae into the blood, completing the cycle. Adults can live 5-10 years in an untreated host.
Direct animal-to-animal transmission does NOT occur; the mosquito is an obligate intermediate host/vector, exactly as stated in the catalogue text.
do_not_draw: A segmented body with visible external rings/grooves like an earthworm (annelid) — nematode cuticle is smooth and continuous.
Proglottids, a scolex, or suckers/hooks on the head — those are tapeworm (cestode) features, a frequent confusion, and do not belong on a nematode.
Jaws, teeth, fangs, or a biting mouth — the mouth is a simple, small, unarmed opening.
Legs, fins, or any appendages — nematodes have none.
The worm shown in the LEFT side of the heart or in a systemic (non-pulmonary) artery — it lives specifically in the right ventricle and pulmonary arteries.
A straight, uncoiled male tail — the coiled/spiral posterior is a defining, checkable male feature.
Blood, gore, open-wound or graphic surgical imagery — this is a veterinary teaching subject for an atlas used by children; show the parasite/life cycle, not a suffering animal.
A sick-looking dog or cat as the main subject — depict the worm/mosquito/prevention routine, not disease symptoms on the animal.
